written.why: A cinema seat written (row, seat number) is a genuine ordered pair: row 5 seat 3 is not row 3 seat 5, and two tickets name the same seat only if both components match.
written.text: Imagine two cinema tickets show the seat as (row, seat number). Sara's ticket says $(x-2,\,3)$ and her brother's ticket says $(5,\,y+1)$, and the cashier says both tickets are for exactly the same seat. Work out the values of $x$ and $y$.

written.why: A bus trip is (from, to): Cairo→Aswan differs from Aswan→Cairo, so X×Y ≠ Y×X holds in the world, and the count is n(X)×n(Y).
written.text: Imagine a bus company has two departure stations, $X=\{\text{Cairo},\text{Giza}\}$, and three destination cities, $Y=\{\text{Alexandria},\text{Luxor},\text{Aswan}\}$. Each trip is written as (departure, destination). Write every possible trip as an ordered pair, and say how many trips there are. Would trips written (destination, departure) be the same list?

written.why: Bus links from stations to towns are naturally drawn as arrows from one group to another and as points on a grid, with direction mattering.
written.text: Suppose a bus company numbers its two starting stations $X=\{1,2\}$ and its three towns $Y=\{3,4,5\}$, and every station has a direct bus to every town. The manager wants a poster of all the routes. Write the routes as ordered pairs, then show how you would draw them with arrows from stations to towns, and as points on a grid.

written.why: A town map with the school as the origin and (blocks east, blocks north) as coordinates makes a point on the plane with quadrants and axes; swapping the numbers gives a different place.
written.text: Imagine a town map where the school is at the centre $(0,0)$ and each place is written (blocks east, blocks north), with negative numbers meaning west or south. A bakery is at $(3,-2)$, a library is at $(-4,3)$ and a park is at $(0,-3)$. Mark them on a grid and say which quadrant or axis each one is in.

checked.why: x-2=5 gives x=7 and y+1=3 gives y=2. It uses only equal pairs. A (row, seat) ticket really does depend on order, because row 5 seat 3 is not row 3 seat 5.

The 6 pairs and n=6 are correct. The point fails. Writing (destination, departure) describes the same six trips with the labels swapped, so it is only notation. In the world it is the same list, but the maths says Y×X is different. The reversed pairs would also put Luxor or Aswan as a departure station, which is not one.
X×Y has the 6 pairs (1,3),(1,4),(1,5),(2,3),(2,4),(2,5). Each route is one arrow from a station to a town and one grid point. This matches the objective's arrow and cartesian diagrams.

(3,-2) is in the fourth quadrant. (-4,3) is in the second quadrant. (0,-3) is on the y-axis. Swapping east and north gives a different place, so order matters in the real map. The coordinate plane is the objective's own method.

written.why: No lesson story. A taxi fare gives a rule b = 2a + 4 from distance to fare, and (distance, fare) is not (fare, distance), so order of the pair is real.
written.text: Imagine a taxi that charges 4 pounds to start, plus 2 pounds for each kilometre. Let $X=\{1,2,3\}$ be the trip lengths in km and $Y=\{6,8,10,12\}$ the possible fares in pounds, with $a\,R\,b$ meaning «$b = 2a + 4$». Write the relation $R$ as a set of ordered pairs (trip length, fare).

written.why: No lesson story. Which student reads which type of book is a real pairing with a direction (student to book type), matching the book's own arrow-diagram idea.
written.text: Suppose three friends, Ali, Mona and Omar, each read some types of books from the school library: Ali reads Science and Culture, Mona reads History, and Omar reads Literature. Here $X$ is the set of friends, $Y$ is the set of book types, and «reads» connects them. Draw this relation as an arrow diagram from each friend to the book types they read, and then as a cartesian diagram.

written.why: No lesson story. A bakery gives all possible (buyer, item) pairs as X × Y, while what was actually bought is only some of them, so the relation is a subset of X × Y; order matters since (buyer, item) is not (item, buyer).
written.text: Imagine a bakery where two customers, Salma and Ahmed, can each buy bread, cake or biscuits. Let $X=\{\text{Salma},\text{Ahmed}\}$ and $Y=\{\text{bread},\text{cake},\text{biscuits}\}$. Suppose Salma bought bread and cake, and Ahmed bought only biscuits. List every possible pair (customer, item) in $X\times Y$, then decide which of them belong to the relation «bought» and whether this relation is a subset of $X\times Y$.

checked.why: b=2a+4 gives 1→6, 2→8, 3→10, so R={(1,6),(2,8),(3,10)}. All values are in Y, and 12 is simply unused. It uses only this objective's method. The taxi fare is a clearly hypothetical, plausible story. Swapping the pair gives (fare, length), which is a different real relation, so order matters.

The relation is {(Ali,Science),(Ali,Culture),(Mona,History),(Omar,Literature)}. It is drawn as an arrow diagram and a cartesian diagram, as the objective asks. The names are invented and the setting is simple. Reversing the direction gives book type → reader, which is a different real relation, so direction matters.

X×Y has 2×3=6 pairs. «bought» is {(Salma,bread),(Salma,cake),(Ahmed,biscuits)}, which is a subset of X×Y. This matches the objective, and the story is hypothetical. A pair (item, customer) would belong to Y×X, which is a genuinely different thing.

written.why: Each student rides one school bus, so pairing student → bus is truly a function; a student listed with two buses breaks it, and reversing (bus → student) would not be one since a bus carries many students.
written.text: Imagine three students, Ali, Mona and Omar, and a school-bus list that pairs each student with the bus line they ride. List 1 is $\{(\text{Ali}, 5), (\text{Mona}, 7), (\text{Omar}, 5)\}$. List 2 is $\{(\text{Ali}, 5), (\text{Mona}, 7), (\text{Mona}, 9), (\text{Omar}, 5)\}$. Which list could be a real timetable where every student has one bus, and how can you tell by looking at the first element of each pair?

written.why: Loaves → price is a rule where each number of loaves has exactly one price, so it is a function that can be written as f(x)=y, as pairs, and drawn.
written.text: Suppose a bakery sells each loaf of bread for $3$ pounds, and you buy $1$, $2$, $3$ or $4$ loaves. Let $X=\{1,2,3,4\}$ be the number of loaves and let $f$ give the price in pounds. Write this as $f : X \to Y$ with $f(x)=3x$, list the ordered pairs, and draw it as an arrow diagram and a cartesian diagram.

written.why: Teams → goals scored is a function; the possible goal counts form the codomain, but only the goals actually scored form the range, a subset of it.
written.text: Imagine a football round where Team A scored $1$ goal, Team B scored $3$ goals and Team C scored $1$ goal. The fixture sheet allows scores of $0, 1, 2$ or $3$ goals. Let $X=\{A,B,C\}$ and $Y=\{0,1,2,3\}$, with $f$ pairing each team with its goals, so $f=\{(A,1),(B,3),(C,1)\}$. What are the domain, the codomain and the range of $f$, and why is the range smaller than the codomain?

numbers.working: Images of A, B, C are 1, 3, 1; repeats counted once

checked.why: List 1 has the first elements Ali, Mona and Omar, each once, so it is a function. In List 2 Mona appears twice, with 7 and 9, so one student has two images and it is not a function. In the real timetable a student with two buses breaks the 'one bus each' rule, so the maths matches the world. Only the objective's idea is used and the names are generic.

f(x)=3x gives f={(1,3),(2,6),(3,9),(4,12)}. Each number of loaves has exactly one price, which is why it is a function in the real shop too. The codomain Y is not stated, but a student can take Y={3,6,9,12} or a larger set. The notation, ordered pairs, arrow diagram and cartesian diagram are all this objective's work.

The domain is {A,B,C}, the codomain is {0,1,2,3} and the range is {1,3}. The range is smaller because no team scored 0 or 2 goals, so those allowed scores are not images. If the pairing is reversed, a score of 1 goal maps to both A and C, which is not a function. That matches the world, because a score does not identify one team.

written.why: The lesson has no story; a profit rule written as a sum of powers of x gives a function whose degree is read from the highest power.
written.text: Imagine a bakery owner who models her daily profit, in pounds, from selling $x$ trays of bread with the rule $P(x)=5+3x-2x^3$. Her assistant says the rule is a polynomial, and her cousin says it is a function of the second degree. Which of them is right: is it a polynomial, and what is its degree?

written.why: No lesson story. A price rule depending on the side of a square plate lets the student substitute a whole number and a surd.
written.text: Suppose a workshop charges $f(x)=x^2-x+3$ pounds for engraving a square plate whose side is $x$ dm. Imagine one plate has side $2$ dm and another has side $\sqrt{3}$ dm. What does each plate cost, that is, what are $f(2)$ and $f(\sqrt{3})$?

written.why: No lesson story. A taxi fare with a starting charge plus a fixed price per km is a first-degree rule whose graph is a straight line.
written.text: Suppose a taxi charges $5$ pounds to start the ride plus $3$ pounds for each kilometre, so the fare is $f(x)=3x+5$ for a ride of $x$ km. Imagine you want to show the fare for any distance on a graph. Which ordered pairs would you find for $x=0,1,2$, and what shape do they make when you draw them?

written.why: No lesson story. Fencing a rectangle with fixed perimeter gives a downward-opening quadratic, whose vertex is the true best (maximum) area.
written.text: Suppose a farmer has $20$ m of fence and makes a rectangular garden with width $x$ m. The length must then be $10-x$ m, so the area is $f(x)=x(10-x)=-x^2+10x$ square metres. Imagine drawing the graph of this function. Where is its vertex, what is the axis of symmetry, and what is the largest area the farmer can get?

numbers.working: perimeter 20 = 2(x + length), so length = 10 - x; area = x(10-x) = -x^2+10x

checked.why: P(x)=5+3x-2x^3 is a polynomial and its highest power is 3, so its degree is 3. The assistant is right and the cousin's 'second degree' is wrong. This uses only the objective's definition. The cubic profit model is plainly an imagined one. The degree is read from the rule, not from how it is written.

The values are f(2)=4-2+3=5 and f(√3)=3-√3+3=6-√3≈4.27. The maths fits the objective's worked example. But the story makes a workshop charge an irrational amount, 6-√3 pounds, which no real price can be. The cost rule also falls as the plate grows from 0 to 0.5 dm, which is odd for an engraving charge. The surd is forced into a context where it is not realistic.

f(0)=5, f(1)=8, f(2)=11, giving the pairs (0,5), (1,8), (2,11). They lie on a straight line, which is a linear function with a=3 and b=5. The taxi fare of a start charge plus a per-km rate really does rise by a constant amount per km, so the straight line is a property of the real fare.

20 m of fence gives width plus length = 10, so the length is 10-x and the area is -x²+10x. Here a=-1 and b=10, so the vertex is at x=-b/2a=5 and f(5)=25. The vertex is (5,25), the axis is x=5, and the maximum area is 25 m², which is the 5 m by 5 m square. The downward-opening curve matches the real fact that the area has a largest value.
